newsitem.title: USA: Western floods bog down NYMEX electricity complex.
newsitem.headline: Western floods bog down NYMEX electricity complex.

text.p: Growing worries over excess hydroelectric generation in the western U.S. have dampened prices in the New York Mercantile Exchange's electricity futures contracts, industry sources said.
"People are looking at the hydro situation. They don't want to be long," said a Houston futures trader.

Recent heavy rain and snow out West, while flooding parts of northern California and causing billions of dollars in damage, left ample hydro resources for power generation at least through the spring, market sources said.

The U.S. Bureau of Reclamation, pointing out the rainy season is only half over in California, said this week that federally-owned hydroelectric dams in the state are running full-out to make room in reservoirs for future rainfall.
The agency operates 12 hydropower plants, whose generating capacity total 5,000 gigawatt hours a year, in the district comprised of California, southern Oregon and western Nevada.
The agency said it tried to speed up the return of some hydroturbines, currently down for maintenance, to take advantage of the strong runoffs.

Concerns over the hydro situation out West have begun to mitigate the direct influence that NYMEX's Henry Hub natural gas futures exerted over the power market in December, when rising gas prices drove up the cost of generating electricity.
"There's excess hydro. That would offset the relationship between electricity and gas," said Corey Bell, analyst at Dean Witter Reynolds.
An overabundance of hydropower discourages gas usage for generating electricty.
The spot California-Oregon Border electricity contract lost more than half of its value in a month, trading at midday Thursday at $14.05 per Megawatt hour, compared with a peak of $28.85 December 5.
Volume has remained fairly constant, however, at about 200 contracts a day.
Bonneville Power Administration (BPA), the federal agency that markets output from the Northwest's vast system of dams this week began offering aggressively priced "market expansion" power.
BPA usually gives those discounts to selected customers during periods of abundant hydroelectric production.
Analysts and traders noted Henry Hub futures have been driven this week by forecasts of frigid temperatures in the midwestern and eastern U.S.
But weather in the West, with exception of eastern Arizona and New Mexico, has not triggered much heating demand.
Some traders said the recent rainfall, especially in northern California, washed away some of the snowpack that had built up earlier at lower elevations.
State officials nevertheless report that the low lying snowpack is still well-above the seasonal average, with some counties reporting it over 200 percent above normal.
